newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian gunman jailed "for term of natural life".
newsitem.headline: Australian gunman jailed "for term of natural life".

text.p: An Australian court on Friday sentenced Port Arthur killer Martin Bryant to life in jail for the shooting massacre of 35 people at a tourist site in the southern island state of Tasmania in April.
Judge William Cox in the Tasmanian Supreme Court ordered that Bryant, 29, should be held in jail "for the term of his natural life".

Bryant confessed two weeks ago to unleashing modern Australia's worst mass murder among the ruins of a former penal colony at Port Arthur on April 28. He had earlier pleaded not guilty, insisting that he went surfing that day.
"Objectively, it is difficult to imagine a more chilling catalogue of crime," said Cox as he passed sentence.
In hearings this week, the court was told how Bryant killed 12 people in just 15 seconds, shooting them as they sat having lunch in a tourist cafe and ignoring pleas for mercy.
A total of 20 people died in the cafe and by the time of Bryant's arrest 35 people were dead and Tasmania was in a state of profound shock.
The court has heard that Bryant is a mentally disturbed man of restricted intelligence who appeared to suffer a rare personality disorder called Asperger's Syndrome.
But psychiatric reports quoted in court said Bryant was not criminally insane and knew right from wrong.
"The repercussion of this crime has been worldwide," Cox told the court on Friday.
Bryant smirked, as he has done on previous courtroom appearances, and stifled a giggle, but chose to remain silent.
The judge described Bryant as someone of severely-limited intellgence who had been abnormal since childhood and later developed into a "pathetic social misfit".
"From an early age, he has displayed severe development problems, being grossly disturbed from childhood," he said.
"I have ... every reason to fear that he will remain indefinitely as disturbed and insensitive as he was when he committed the crimes," he said.
Cox accepted that although Bryant's intellectual capacity bordered on mental disability he was not insane.
"He knew what he was doing and that it was something that he ought not to do," he said.
The courtroom was, as it has been throughout the week-long sentencing hearing, packed with distraught massacre survivors and relatives of the victims.
Some wiped away tears as Bryant, seemingly untroubled by the sentence, was led away from the dock for the last time.
Bryant's lawyer said this week that his client expected to spend the rest of his life in prison.
